points.en: Money is a good servant that feeds families, supports the gospel and relieves the poor, but a cruel master once it takes the throne of the heart; the danger is the love of money, not money itself.
Contentment is Scripture's weapon against money's mastery: the contented person has broken its power and can use money rather than be used by it.
No one can serve both God and mammon (Matthew 6:24); godliness with contentment is great gain (1 Timothy 6).
The prosperity gospel teaches that God wills every faithful believer to be materially rich and healthy, and that poverty or sickness shows weak faith.
Jesus lived in material humility: no home, born in a manger, borrowed colt, upper room and tomb, His only possession gambled away.
If wealth showed the Father's favor, the perfectly faithful Son of God would have been the most poorly rewarded of all.
Jesus blessed the poor (poor in spirit; Luke: 'Blessed are you poor') and pronounced woe on the rich, the reverse of the prosperity teacher.
He warned that it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom, like a camel through a needle's eye.
So a message promising wealth offers a blessing Christ never gave and ignores a warning He plainly gave.
Giving is grounded in the gospel: Christ, though rich, became poor so we could become rich, so we give because we first received.
Giving must be free, glad and from the heart, not grudging or compelled; God loves a cheerful giver.
This rules out manipulative fundraising, guilt-driven appeals and emotional pressure on people to give.
God promises the generous giver sufficiency and the means for every good work (2 Corinthians 9:8).
He does not promise personal luxury or riches; He resupplies the giver to keep giving, not to hoard.
Caring for the poor is not an optional add-on but the gospel showing its hands and feet; faith that offers only kind words to the hungry is dead (James 2).
What we do for the least of Christ's brethren we do to Christ Himself (Matthew 25:40).
Failing to help is sin: the rich man who stepped over Lazarus did nothing, a sin comfortable churches commit.
Help the poor with wise, personal, dignifying love that sees the person, remembering the poor bear God's image.
Wealth in a Christian's hand is a trust to be shared, not a reward to be displayed; God gives resources so that we may share them.
A pastor living in luxury while his members languish in poverty is a scandal who has inverted God's purpose; his own lifestyle should model contentment and generosity.
1 John 3:17: shutting up one's heart from a brother in need cannot coexist with the love of God.
The danger is the love of money, not money itself: the grip of money on the heart, not the amount in the hand.
So a poor person can idolize money as much as a rich one; the question is never how much one has but whom one serves.
The rich man's sin was neglect, not active harm: he stepped over the beggar at his gate day after day and did nothing while feasting.
A comfortable church commits this same sin constantly, and it is serious (it damns).
The poor man at the door bears God's image as fully as we do, calling for wise, dignifying love rather than sentimentality.
Contentment frees a believer from money's power, since there is nothing it can promise that he is desperate to buy.
Practically, he works honestly, handles debt with sober care, saves prudently and gives joyfully, using money rather than being used by it.
